options.label: Database table with admin UI
options.tradeoff: Gives sales/support ownership and an audit trail, but requires a migration and UI work.
options.description: Per-customer overrides live next to other customer data; changes are logged and reversible.

options.label: Redis key per customer
options.tradeoff: Instantly tunable by ops, but no audit trail and can be lost or mis-typed.
options.description: Engineers/SRE can change limits without deploy; risk of untracked config drift.

options.tradeoff: Simplest today, but requires an engineer and deploy for every change.

questions.question: What response should a throttled client receive?

options.label: HTTP 429 with Retry-After and JSON error body
options.tradeoff: Standard and script-friendly, but requires a small response-format change.
options.description: `{ error: 'rate_limit_exceeded', retry_after: 12 }` with RFC-compliant header.

options.label: Plain-text HTTP 429
options.tradeoff: Simple to implement, but harder for automated clients to parse.
options.description: Just `429 Too Many Requests` with a text body.

options.label: HTTP 503 Service Unavailable
options.tradeoff: Signals overload but is semantically wrong and breaks client retry expectations.
options.description: Clients may treat it as server fault rather than a self-imposed limit.

brief.where: server.ts currently returns 401 for missing header, 201/200 for success, 404 otherwise. No 429 handling exists.
brief.what: Define the HTTP contract when a request exceeds the rate limit.
brief.how: A 429 with Retry-After lets scripted clients back off correctly. 503 implies server error and can trigger the wrong client behavior.

questions.question: How should we roll this out without breaking enterprise integrations?

options.label: Shadow/monitor mode first, then enforce
options.tradeoff: Safest path but delays protection by days/weeks while you gather burst data.
options.description: Log what would be rejected; set limits based on observed enterprise patterns; then flip to enforce.

options.label: Enforce immediately with a high default limit
options.tradeoff: Fast protection, but outliers above the high limit still break.
options.description: Set a generous ceiling (e.g., derived from last week's peak) and lower it over time.

options.label: Enterprise opt-out initially, then tighten
options.tradeoff: Protects the database quickly but creates two classes of customers.
options.description: Enterprise customers bypass limits at first; remove opt-out after negotiating per-customer limits.

brief.where: PLAN.md wants to ship this week. Enterprise customers currently burst legitimately; breaking them is a churn risk.
brief.what: Choose the deployment sequence and customer communication.
brief.how: Monitor-first lets you set evidence-based limits. Enforce-first protects the DB sooner but risks rejecting valid enterprise traffic before you know what those traffic patterns are.

questions.question: Should rate limiting apply only to POST /orders, or should GET /orders also count toward the limit?

options.label: POST /orders only
options.tradeoff: Protects the expensive write path with minimal breakage risk, but leaves cheap reads unbounded.
options.description: Matches the incident (40k writes) and keeps list endpoints unrestricted.

options.label: Both POST and GET under one shared budget
options.tradeoff: Prevents any customer from dominating the instance, but may break polling scripts.
options.description: A single budget consumed by both routes; cheapest reads can starve writes.

options.label: Separate budgets for POST and GET
options.tradeoff: Granular protection at the cost of more configuration and mental overhead.
options.description: Two independent limits; e.g., 100 POST/min and 1000 GET/min.

brief.where: PLAN.md says POST /orders writes to Postgres and is expensive; GET /orders is cheap. Current server.ts handles both with no limits.
brief.what: Decide which routes consume rate-limit budget.
brief.how: Limiting only POST directly prevents the recent 40k-orders incident. Including GET protects against read abuse but may throttle legitimate polling and complicates the limit story for enterprise customers.

questions.question: Should we key the rate limit on x-customer-id, client IP, or both?

options.label: x-customer-id only
options.tradeoff: Matches existing auth and is simple, but a customer can distribute requests across many hosts under one ID.
options.description: Uses the header server.ts already requires. Enterprise bursts from a single host are naturally allowed.

options.label: x-customer-id + client IP combined
options.tradeoff: Catches distributed abuse but over-limits customers behind NATs or proxies.
options.description: A customer with 10 servers gets 10x the aggregate budget of a customer with one server.

options.label: Client IP only
options.tradeoff: Ignores the authenticated tenant model and is easy to evade via proxies.
options.description: Wrong fit because x-customer-id is already the trusted customer identity.

brief.where: server.ts already requires x-customer-id. The incident was one customer ID creating 40k orders. Client IP is available from Bun's request but unused.
brief.what: Choose the dimension that identifies a 'user' for rate-limit accounting.
brief.how: Customer ID aligns with the existing tenant model. IP keying catches multi-host abuse but breaks NAT/proxy scenarios and misattributes shared egress points.

questions.question: Which rate-limiting algorithm should we use?

options.label: Token bucket
options.tradeoff: Supports scripted bursts and is simple to implement, but allows short spikes up to bucket capacity.
options.description: Good fit for enterprise scripts that legitimately burst and then go idle.

options.label: Sliding window log
options.tradeoff: Fair and accurate, but higher Redis memory and operation cost.
options.description: Stores a timestamp per request; precise but expensive at high throughput.

options.label: Fixed window
options.tradeoff: Simplest and lowest resource use, but causes stampedes at window boundaries.
options.description: A customer can do 2x the intended rate by straddling a window edge.

brief.where: PLAN.md lists fixed window, sliding window, or token bucket as undecided. Enterprise customers legitimately burst.
brief.what: Pick the counter algorithm that enforces the limit.
brief.how: Token bucket naturally accommodates bursts; fixed window has boundary-stampede risk that could recreate overload; sliding window is fairest but costs more per request.

options.label: Redis cluster
options.tradeoff: Consistent global limits across all instances, but adds a dependency and small latency.
options.description: Uses the existing Redis 7 cluster already shared with another service.

options.label: In-memory per instance
options.tradeoff: Fast and simple, but a customer under round-robin gets 3x the effective budget.
options.description: Each of the 3 instances maintains its own counters with no cross-instance coordination.

options.label: Redis with local short-lived cache
options.tradeoff: Reduces Redis load, but counters can be slightly stale and inconsistent.
options.description: Hybrid approach; more complex and harder to reason about under edge cases.

brief.where: There are 3 Bun server instances behind a round-robin load balancer. Redis 7 cluster exists and is used by another service.
brief.what: Decide whether counters are centralized or local.
brief.how: Redis gives a single source of truth, which matters when a customer can hit any instance. In-memory under round-robin effectively triples budgets and lets one customer still overload Postgres.
